property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(newOwner), the contract's public owner() becomes exactly the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin, so when the caller is a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) the mutant yields owner() == tx.origin while the reference yields owner() == the provided newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) updates the public owner() to newOwner; the mutant that omits the state assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some input owner/newOwner choices.

For any caller address a that is currently the contract owner, after calling setOwner(b) the contract's public owner() equals b (reference preserves assignment for all admissible inputs; the mutant that omits the assignment can be detected because for some fuzzed b the owner() will not equal b).

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOwner(x) sets owner to the provided argument x (reference); the mutant instead sets owner to the caller (msg.sender), so there exist inputs where owner() != the provided _owner after the call.

For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that overwrites owner with address(0) violates this because for some fuzzed newOwner values the final owner becomes address(0) instead of the supplied value.

For any caller address A and target _owner address X, when A calls setOwner(X) the reference contract C allows the call to succeed iff A == C.owner(), so after the call C.owner() == X; the mutant inverts the owner check and therefore will allow non-owners to call setOwner and will block the real owner, causing C.owner() to differ for some inputs.

For all caller and target pairs, only the current owner can successfully call setOwner on the correct contract (so after the call, owner equals the target iff the caller was the prior owner); the mutant inverts the check, allowing non-owners to succeed and blocking the real owner, so there exist caller/target inputs where owner differs between reference and mutant.

Invariant: only the current owner can change owner via setOwner, so after any call to setOwner by any address other than the current owner, the owner remains unchanged; the mutant removes the require and thus allows non-owners to change owner.

The contract always allows only the immediate caller (msg.sender) who is the current owner to successfully change owner; replacing msg.sender with tx.origin allows an indirect (contract) caller to bypass restriction and change owner for some inputs.
